ranges.quote: This is episode 19 of exploring really cool tech. Today, we'll be talking about approximate counters and eventual consistency.
ranges.reason: HOOK VARIANT B (cool-tech framing). Only take of this framing, and clean from the first word -- no ASR box padding at its head.

ranges.quote: So when you look at a Ronaldo post, that like count isn't exact, and that's actually the smart design choice.
ranges.reason: Only take. ASR boxes 'choice.' to 43.10 against an acoustic end of 42.67.

ranges.quote: Here's the problem. If every like had to instantly update one perfectly accurate number, that single row becomes a bottleneck. Millions of people liking at once would all fight to write to the same place.
ranges.reason: Single clean take. The 480ms beat after 'bottleneck.' is the turn inside the beat and is where the overlay's second act starts.

ranges.quote: So at massive scale, we relax. Likes are counted across many servers and added up, with the displayed number trailing slightly behind reality.
This is eventual consistency. The count converges to correct in seconds, but in any instant, it might be approximate.
ranges.reason: Single clean take. Split from the next range at the 510ms gap after 'approximate.'

ranges.quote: For likes, nobody cares if it briefly says a million instead of a million three.
ranges.reason: Contiguous in the source, kept separate so the 'nobody cares' example gets its own overlay instead of being buried in the eventual-consistency beat.

ranges.quote: Speed and availability matter far more than perfect accuracy. Your bank balance, of course, gets the opposite treatment.
ranges.reason: Single clean take. The 690ms beat before 'Your bank balance' is the pivot the overlay's likes-vs-bank contrast cut lands on.

ranges.quote: At a billion likes, close enough beats exactly right. Next episode, we'll talk about how computers understand meaning.
ranges.reason: Only take. DROPPED: an off-script aside at 95.30-97.86 ('Let me know if you want me to talk more about this in a future episode') that sits between TRADEOFF and PAYOFF -- it breaks the tight close the series uses and is not in the script.

_windows_note: Output-timeline windows on render.py's real 24fps extract grid: each segment's rendered duration is ceil((end-start)*24)/24, not the raw source span. Verified against rendered clips where measurable. Overlay start_in_output values are derived from THESE numbers.
_variant: Variant B -- 'exploring really cool tech' intro.
_overlay_gap_audit: Gaps >= 0.5s are deliberate returns to the talking head (ep13 shipped 1.0-6.7s gaps at 49-54% coverage). Anything shorter is closed to exactly zero, per rule 12 -- a sub-half-second hole reads as a bare-footage flash, not a breath. EP19 tradeoff->payoff is contiguous for exactly this reason: its beats butt up against each other and a 0.3s gap would have landed on the punchline.
_zoom_note: Gradual CENTERED zoom on the talking head. focal (540,960) = exact frame centre, not render.py's eye-line default. Direction alternates per segment so each range starts at the scale the previous one ended on -- the drift is continuous across every cut instead of snapping back to 1.0 at each edit. Magnitude capped at 4.5%: the overlays were placed against measured face positions with clearances as tight as 40px, and a centered zoom displaces a point by distance_from_centre*(Z-1), so 4.5% costs the tightest one ~13px while 12% would cost it ~35px and push graphics into the face.
_title_note: EP19 uses a TikTok-native text-box title INSTEAD of the house title card (slot_title) -- a swap, not an addition: the boxes sit where the house card's top-left block lives. Each VARIANT gets its own title composition because the on-screen title must match that variant's SPOKEN hook: A says 'MASTERING SYSTEM DESIGN', B says 'EXPLORING REALLY COOL TECH'. Using one title for both would put a title on screen contradicting the narration and defeat the point of A/B-ing the hooks. Revert = point back at slot_title at 0.000/2.766.
